title: Morning (II.10)
hook: before the phone lights up, Francis de Sales asks for a few minutes: thank, look ahead, and hand the day over
tomorrow: the day went badly. why does Francis start the night with thanks?

segments.voice: Last week ended in a garden: a few thoughts picked at the end of prayer and carried all day. The line was a nosegay. Now the book walks into the day itself, from its first minute.

Five-forty. The alarm is off, the room is still dark, and the phone on the nightstand is already glowing: a group chat, an email, a reminder about something due. One swipe and the day has started without you. Francis de Sales, a bishop who wrote the Introduction to the Devout Life for people with jobs and households, asks for a few minutes before any of that. Not the long meditation; that has its own hour. A short exercise for every morning, the rushed ones too. And it ends with a strange move: you hand the day over before you've lived a minute of it.
screen: `FIVE-FORTY, AND THE PHONE IS GLOWING.` → `A FEW MINUTES FIRST.` → `HAND IT OVER BEFORE YOU LIVE IT.`

segments.voice: It comes in four steps. First, adore and thank. Begin, Francis says, by adoring God and thanking him for keeping you through the night, and if anything in the night went wrong, ask pardon. Second, remember what the day is for. This day, he says, is given you so that you can gain the day of eternity, so make a firm resolve to use it well. Third, look ahead. Think through what the day will probably hold: the work, the people, the chances to serve God, and the temptations that could come with them, to anger, to vanity, to some other slip. Then get ready. If you know you'll deal with someone quick to anger, settle now on gentle words. Fourth, the heart in your hands. Humble yourself, he says, knowing you can't carry out these good plans alone. Then take your heart in your hands, as it were, and offer it to God with everything you've resolved, asking him to keep it and strengthen it. He adds that all of it can be done briefly, before you leave your room. Here's the detail to tell a friend tonight: the planning sits third, between the thanks and the offering. It isn't a to-do list. It's a plan made in company.
screen: `ADORE AND THANK.` · `WHAT THE DAY IS FOR.` · `LOOK AHEAD, GET READY.` · `THE HEART IN YOUR HANDS.` · then, large: `PLAN THE DAY WITH GOD.`

segments.voice: Pick one moment in the next day that could go sideways: a meeting, a practice, a hard conversation. Through the sit, decide one way you'll meet it, the way Francis settles on gentle words before seeing someone short-tempered. If you pray, you can end by offering the day, heart in hand.
Morning. In Francis's book, a short exercise to begin the day: thanks, purpose, a look ahead, and an offering.
Your line: plan the day with god. The plan comes after the thanks and before the offering. Until tomorrow.

notes: Introduction II.10 paraphrased: adore God and thank him for preservation through the night, asking pardon for any offense; the present day is given to gain the day of eternity, with a firm purpose to use it well; foresee the affairs, occasions of serving God and temptations (anger, vanity, other irregularities) and prepare means to meet them; humble yourself, knowing you can't do it alone, take your heart in your hands and offer it with your good purposes to God, asking him to protect and strengthen it; this may be done briefly before leaving the room. The 'someone quick to anger' example paraphrases his illustration of preparing gentle words for a meeting; confirm the exact example.
